opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something I think about a lot, because I think the boundaries are getting blurrier in a really interesting way.

Historically, the reason you had these distinct roles is that each one required a lot of specialized, expensive-to-acquire skill just to get anything done. If you were a designer, you could imagine an interface, but turning it into something real meant handing a Figma file to an engineer and waiting. If you were a PM, you could write a spec, but you were a step removed from the actual artifact. And engineers spent a huge share of their time on translation work, taking someone else's intent and turning it into code.

What AI does, especially the coding agents we've seen over the last couple of years, is dramatically lower the cost of that translation step. A designer can now get to a working prototype on their own. A PM can build the thing they're imagining and put it in front of users before anyone writes a formal spec. So the hand-off points that defined these roles start to dissolve.

But I don't think that means everyone becomes a generalist and the roles disappear. What I see instead is that the center of gravity of each role shifts toward judgment. For engineers, less of the job is typing code and more of it is deciding what the system should look like, what the right abstractions are, how to evaluate whether the thing the model produced is actually correct, robust, and secure. For designers, it's less about producing pixel-perfect mocks and more about taste and understanding users deeply. And for product people, the bottleneck becomes knowing what to build and why, because building is getting cheap.

There's another wrinkle that's specific to building AI products. When the core of your product is a model, the behavior *is* the product, and the behavior is shaped by prompts, data, and evals. Who owns that? It's not cleanly engineering, design, or product. In the best teams I've seen, the people writing evals and looking at outputs every day are often product or domain folks, because they have the clearest sense of what "good" looks like. So you get this new hybrid skill set: someone who understands the user, can reason about model behavior, and is technical enough to iterate quickly.

So my prediction is that teams get smaller and more fluid, with more people who span two or three of these traditional roles, and the scarce resource becomes taste and judgment rather than execution capacity. The organizations that adapt fastest will be the ones that stop organizing around hand-offs and start organizing around tight loops between an idea, a working version, and real feedback.

r001.rationale: The response says AI lowers the cost of turning intent into working software, letting designers and product managers build directly and more people span traditional roles.

r002.rationale: It describes engineers spending less effort typing code and more effort deciding on system design, abstractions, and evaluating correctness, robustness, and security.

r003.rationale: It connects cheaper implementation and reduced translation work to individuals building prototypes or products themselves and spanning more of the development process.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and it's one I think about a lot because I think the honest answer is that those boundaries are getting a lot blurrier, and in a lot of cases they're just dissolving.

So if you think about how software has traditionally been built, you've got this kind of relay race. A product person figures out what to build and writes a spec. A designer takes that and turns it into mockups. And then an engineer takes the mockups and writes the code. And each of those handoffs is expensive. There's information lost at every step, there's a lot of back-and-forth, and the whole loop from "I have an idea" to "I can actually see it working" can be weeks.

What AI does, especially coding agents, is it collapses that loop. The cost of actually building the thing drops dramatically. And when building gets cheap, the interesting thing is that the bottleneck moves. It's no longer "can we implement this," it's "do we know what we actually want, and is it any good once we see it." Those are fundamentally product and design questions. So I'd argue that in a lot of teams, engineers are becoming more like product people almost by necessity, because they're the ones sitting closest to the agent, and the agent needs to be told what to build and why. Taste starts to matter a lot more than raw implementation speed.

And it goes the other direction too. A designer or a PM who has a clear idea can now go build a working prototype, not a Figma mockup, an actual thing that runs, and put it in front of users or in front of the team. That changes the conversation completely. You're not debating an abstraction anymore, you're reacting to something real. I've seen that be incredibly powerful, because so much of what makes software good only becomes visible once you can actually touch it.

Now, I want to be careful not to oversell it. I don't think engineering as a discipline goes away. Somebody still has to understand the system, understand the failure modes, know when the agent has produced something that looks right but is going to fall over in production. If anything, the senior engineering skills, architecture, judgment, knowing what "good" looks like, those become more valuable, not less. What gets commoditized is the translation step, turning a well-specified intent into working code.

So where I land is, I think we're moving toward roles that look more like "builder" with a specialization, rather than three separate crafts with walls between them. The best people on a team will be the ones who can hold the whole picture, what the user needs, what it should feel like, and how it should work, and who can direct these tools effectively across all three. The org charts will probably lag reality for a while, but the actual day-to-day work is already changing.

r001.rationale: The response says coding agents lower implementation costs and let people work across product, design, and engineering, but it does not connect this broader scope to programming moving to a higher level of abstraction.

r002.rationale: It describes attention shifting toward product and design judgment as implementation becomes cheaper, but does not identify language or framework details as the effort being displaced.

r003.rationale: The response links cheaper implementation to broader roles and prototyping, but does not explain that reduced cognitive demands give an individual capacity to address more of the overall problem.

astra-6.text:
I think those boundaries are going to become a lot more fluid. Historically, part of the reason we’ve separated product, design, and engineering is that each requires a different set of specialized skills to turn an idea into something that works. AI reduces some of the cost of moving between those activities.

A designer can get much closer to a working implementation. A product manager can build a prototype to test an idea instead of trying to communicate everything through a specification. And an engineer can explore product and design decisions without waiting for every detail to be handed over.

But I don’t think that means the underlying expertise stops mattering. Being able to generate an interface isn’t the same as understanding whether it solves a user’s problem. And being able to generate code isn’t the same as knowing whether a system is reliable.

So I’d expect more people to own a problem from beginning to end, with specialists helping where deeper judgment is needed. The interesting shift is that producing the software becomes easier, which puts more emphasis on deciding what to build and figuring out whether it actually works for people.

r001.rationale: The response says AI makes it easier to move between roles and own a problem end to end, but does not connect that change to programming moving to a higher level of abstraction.

r002.rationale: It emphasizes deciding what to build and whether it works, but does not describe developers shifting effort away from language or framework details.

r003.rationale: It says AI makes producing software easier and reduces the cost of moving between activities, then connects that to people owning problems from beginning to end.

sol-6.1.text:
I think those boundaries are going to become a lot more fluid. Today, you might have a product manager write a spec, a designer create a mockup, and an engineer turn that into working software. AI makes it easier for each of those people to go further across that workflow. A designer can build a working prototype, a product manager can test an idea directly, and an engineer can explore different user experiences without waiting for a handoff.

But getting something working is different from knowing that you’ve built the right thing. As implementation gets cheaper, judgment becomes more valuable: understanding the customer, deciding what matters, and figuring out whether the result is actually good.

So I don’t think everyone becomes interchangeable. I think we’ll see smaller teams where people have a core specialty but can take an idea much further on their own. And the interesting question becomes less ‘Whose job is this?’ and more ‘Who has enough context to make this decision well?’

r001.rationale: The response says AI helps people work across more of the development workflow, but it does not connect this to programming’s rising level of abstraction.

r002.rationale: It says implementation is getting cheaper and judgment is becoming more valuable, but does not describe developers shifting effort away from language or framework details toward higher-level reasoning.

r003.rationale: The response says AI makes it easier for people to go further across the workflow and lets individuals take an idea much further on their own, linking cheaper implementation to broader individual capacity.
